newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: INTERVIEW - Bangladesh draws FDI as image improves.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Bangladesh draws FDI as image improves.

text.p: Bangladesh's Board of Investment (BOI) said on Thursday the country was expecting billions of dollars in foreign direct investment in the next few years, helped by its improving overseas image.

"There is tremendous response from foreign investors in infrastructure. Power sector alone will bring in $1.15 billion in the next two to three years," BOI executive chairman Anisul Huq Chowdhury told Reuters in an interview.
He said agreements worth several hundred million dollars in telecommunications and gas exploration had also been signed.
"There were some negative stereotype images of Bangladesh abroad. But the image is beginning to change...investments are coming," Chowdhury said.
"Our missions abroad are vigorously pursuing economic diplomacy. An international press campaign is on. Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina herself meets investors whenever she visits foreign countries."
Chowdhury said a competitive incentive package, policy reforms and improving economic indicators were attracting the interest of foreign investors.

"The economy achieved 5.6 percent GDP (gross domestic product) growth last year (1996/97 July-June) and is expected to rise to seven percent in next two years. Inflation is low and per-capita income is gradually rising. These are greatly helping to raise (international) interest in us."
Chowdhury said the response from foreign investors in manufacturing was also significant, with the BOI registering investment proposals worth more than $1 billion in the 1996/97 fiscal year.
He said major proposals were in the sectors of textiles, cement, leather and computer software, and that responses came mainly from Singapore, Japan, Britain, India, Taiwan and South Korea.
"But foreign investors were now basically eyeing infrastructure," he said.
He said deals had been struck with foreign companies to set up four barge-mounted power plants, each of 100 megawatts capacity, which would bring in $450 million.
Three more power plants were open for bidding, he said.
Chowdhury said deals worth about $240 million were also signed with foreign cellular telephone operators.
Two of those companies -- Grameen Telephone and TM International Bangladesh (TMIB)-- have begun operations, while another company was expected to begin operations soon.
Grameen Telecom is a joint venture with Norway's Telenor, Japan's Marubeni and Bangladesh's Grameen Telecom. Telekom Malaysia is the foreign partner in TMIB.
The BOI chief said investments worth "several hundred million dollars" would also be forthcoming in gas exploration and development in next few years.
Bangladesh has already contracted out eight exploration blocks to four foreign oil companies and proposals for others were being evaluated.
"The prospect of gas finds has also brightened prospects of investment in gas-based industries like fertiliser and petro-chemicals," Chowdhury said.
The BOI chief said there were major efforts to remove the remaining barriers on foreign investment.
"Electricity shortages and inadequate port facilities are still serious obstacles. Red tape and outdated legal structures are also major complaints. We are addressing these problems," he said.
Chowdhury said the Law Reforms Commission was working on updating laws relating to business transactions, and an administrative reforms committee was developing suggestions for reforming bureaucracy.
A new industrial policy and a fresh telecommunications policy were also in the offing that, Chowdhury said, were expected to further open opportunities for private and foreign investment.
"In the meantime, we have already taken some initiatives to make things easier for foreign investors," Chowdhury said.
He said the BOI was preparing to work as a "one stop" shop where investors would receive help.
"Officials from different service and regulatory agencies like power, telephone and customs would be deputed at BOI so that foreign investors won't have to go to different offices."
